It could be the case that you lose the entire market."

Martin Casado:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that, because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. 

The biggest shift with AI is I can take 20 people, give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Do they make 500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new.

We've turned this into a capital resourcing problem, and we're capital allocators. We're in this very strategic position to help drive the future in a much more direct way than we ever have been before.

If you look at Anthropic and OpenAI, they've probably raised more money in aggregate than the entire downstream ecosystem combined. 

They are these mechanisms of turning money into growth."

tweets.text:
a16z's Martin Casado on the four mindsets people bring to investing, and why knowing yours stops you from justifying your own bias:

1. Financial

"The correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances. That's what it is. What are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? That is a proxy for the entire business."

2. Productive

"You believe you're investing in a productive asset, and the productive asset is what's creating value. If you believe in that, as it creates value, it will create market... The type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like, what is the technical approach? What are the adjacent markets?"

3. Frontier

"I think this is the romantic, idealized version of VC from the 60s and 70s, which is kind of YOLO. It's like, founders know better than VCs, and they've seen something that I don't see, and they're gonna go out there and do it. And, like, who am I to second guess them?"

4. Speculative

"It is always so surprising how prevalent it is... They don't even care about the asset. They just want to time a market, right?... They're like, 'Well, this looks cheap. It's clearly gonna go up in value' or, 'This is the top of the market, like, I'm gonna get out.'"

"...You can justify any deal or not justify any deal. So if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just kind of justify whatever personal bias you have."

@martin_casado w/ @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

"People have been connecting their cards, their credit cards, and their bank accounts via Plaid since the Venmo era. But when you ask them, they're like, 'Oh, yes, I'm very concerned about trust and safety.'"

"I think an example though of where consumers are very concerned about sort of trust and assumptions is around being embarrassed and social signaling... The social mechanics actually feel so much higher stakes than the actual, like, real-world implications."

"[One company] offered a million dollars worth of pizza to anyone that wanted to use their product... In order to get that $30 of pizza, you were granting access to your entire Google Workspace, all of your emails, all of your data for 30 bucks."

"It just proves it right there, that people are willing to just give up all that data for some free pizza."

The era of massive Big Tech stock buybacks is over.

Combined buybacks by Alphabet, $GOOGL, Amazon, $AMZN, Microsoft, $MSFT, Meta, $META, and Oracle, $ORCL, fell to $4.4 billion in Q3 2026, the lowest since Q3 2017.

This comes as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle have not purchased their own stock in 2026.

By comparison, combined buybacks by these Big Tech companies stood at +$33.0 billion in Q1 2026.

AI spending is coming at the expense of Big Tech buybacks.

$COHR earnings transcript TLDR:

Q: On $LITE + $MRVL merger.

A. Customers will prefer an independent optical supplier without competitive conflicts (opportunity for other merchant laser suppliers)

Q: Loop Capital asked about 2028 laser industry oversupply.

A: No oversupply risk by 2028. Coherent’s entire current internal InP production is consumed by its own products while its expanding capacity.

Q: On Chinese laser competition for CPO UHP lasers

A: “We really only have one competitor” (hinting at $LITE). 

Q: On financing concerns for capacity expansion during this market scare

A: Customer LTAs have prepayments, which are used for product capacity orders

2027 completely sold out, LTAs extend to 2030, customers placing orders into 2028.

Q: On laser technology for CPO scale up from Bernstein, whether it’s VCSELs or CW lasers.

A: CW for CPO scale out and scale up for 2026-2027.

2029-2030 sees scale in and chip to chip using micro-VCSELs, and 2028 opportunities for NPO scale up.

So technology of choice is CW for CPO.

- Coherent is seeing pricing power and raising margin targets, supporting view optical players get additional leverage for margin expansion

- Massive new $20B 5Y LTA, anchored by UHP CW lasers, with other optical products mixed in

- demand comes from growth in DC and conversion of copper interconnects to optics. The latter is bandwidth requirements, independent of DC growth.

slower compute growth can coexist with sharply rising optical content per system

TLDR:

- nothing quite showing optical demand like $20B in LTAs anchored by high power lasers from 1 customer alone (not your frontier labs type commitments)

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

And obviously haircut growth valuations (but not to the point where demand collapses to 0).

Yet we're seeing everything in AI trade is getting lumped up together as something that requires heavy financing + not profitable.

I can only reply to a minority of comments, and it’s usually luck-of-the-draw what I see when I’m online. And Twitter isn’t really the best place for long-form debates.

“Why do you think the legal system couldn’t prevent the Biden Admin from allowing millions of unknown foreign men to illegally enter the country?”

-Surely you’re aware of the asymmetry that courts are more able to block specific illegal actions than force officials to take positive actions that require funding. In other words, with a stroke of a pen a court can say,“no, those tariffs are illegal actually, you can’t use emergency powers for indefinite and broad new taxes” but it’s much harder to say, “you have to allocate more resources to the border.” To fix the latter you generally need an executive and legislative branch with the will to do it, which is partially what the 2024 election was a mandate on.

“Why can’t the legal system prevent criminals who’ve been arrested 37 times from being let back into society?”

-Places where people are arrested 37 times tend to be cities where the politicians and courts are in agreement. That’s the set of policies they have on the books and how the rules are being interpreted. If people get fed up with it they can elect people that will write and interpret stricter laws and sentences about repeated crime.

“Why couldn’t the legal system prevent billions of dollars of egregious welfare fraud?”

-Tons of cases are prosecuted each year. Even so, outright fraud is a small share of the spending. The bigger issue is healthcare bloat and demographics.

“Why can’t the legal system enact voter ID which is the most obvious and basic tenet of election security?”

-It’s not the role of the legal system to enact voter ID or other details around voting. That’s primarily within the legislative branch (unless the legislative branch does something that violates the Constitution).

“If you are so willing to label Trump a "fascist", perhaps you could assign a label to the people who fail to deliver the most basic functions of government? What label should they be given?”

-By definition, that description would be closer to anarchist.

I'll summarize my views: 

- tariffs were dumb and a huge unforced error. even if economic impact was largely de minimis, they are still an easy target for the left

- Trump crypto ventures: obviously a huge problem and a foreseeable mistake. I personally objected to this loudly, even before he was elected (look up my name and WLF or the trump memecoin in google news). I was very critical on this point  

- immigration: I support the crackdown, think Trump could have done it more elegantly, but undeniably he delivered on what he said he would, no complaints. maybe was unpopular due to inherent demographics of this country, but not something I am complaining about. 

- Iran war: unforced error. Though I support what he is doing, I think he should have gone much harder much quicker, rather than leave us with this stalemate causing high gas prices. Optics disaster undeniably. 

- Affordability: his decisions didn't help at the margin, but in terms of economic growth (not solely within his control), he has been pretty good. The economy isn't as bad as people think it is. 

- AI: WH hasn't done much one way or the other. Dems have the benefit of being the AI skeptic and datacenter skeptic party. They are on the wrong side of that in my view, but it is politically popular for now.

tweets.text:
Huge relief for $MARA.

FERC approved $MARA’s Long Ridge acquisition today (EC26-92). Good to see the IMM’s spurious BlackRock/Vanguard challenge get the Heisman. FERC also turned down the request to condition approval on keeping the plant’s output in PJM. Solid.

The deal: $1.512B enterprise value for ~0.5 GW of gas generation (485 MW authorized, 505 MW nameplate) and ~$144M of annualized adj. EBITDA, about 10.5x. Recent PJM gas plant deals went at about 7x (Talen 6.7x, Vistra 7x, NRG 7.5x), which would put the plant alone at ~$1.0B. MARA is paying ~$0.5B more for the land, gas wells, rail and expansion option. MARA keeps ~$900M of Long Ridge debt in place and needs ~$610M of cash, which the $600M of BTC-backed loans it drew in August are meant to cover. I’d expect it to close by the Nov 30 outside date.

Debt math: ~$1.9B of MARA’s $2.3B convert stack is zero coupon, so total post-close cash interest is roughly $140M: ~$58M on the Coinbase and Two Prime loans, ~$76M on Long Ridge’s own debt (the 8.75% notes alone are $52.5M) and ~$7M on the converts. Judging the deal on its own: the debt that finances it (Long Ridge’s ~$76M plus ~$46M on the new BTC loans) costs ~$123M a year against $144M of EBITDA, about 1.2x. The upside is expansion.

MARA talks about 600 gross MW of AI load at the site. That appears to include the existing 200 MW of grid load (on top of the 505 MW plant that sells into PJM). AEP’s 2025 filing proposed reconductoring the feeder serving a customer at the Hannibal station to go from 100 to 200 MW, for about $0.5M, targeting about nine months from PJM first seeing the need to in-service. The station ties into four 138 kV lines and once fed a 540 MW smelter, which is encouraging, but nothing is signed. To get from 200 to 600 MW, AEP would likely need to add a second feed or upgrade lines, or MARA would build on-site generation, which raises turbine availability questions. I can’t find a public study of how much more the grid connection can carry. AEP Ohio’s data center tariff also requires large customers to pay for at least 85% of contracted capacity for up to 12 years, if it applies here. Still, an energized site with fuel, land and a 138 kV hub may beat waiting in ERCOT’s queue.

It’s unclear whether the Hannibal buildout goes through the Starwood JV, where MARA would keep up to 50%. That will decide how much of the 600 MW upside MARA owns. Each 100MW developed at a 7% cap rate and $2M/MW rent could be $1.5B+ of value creation, so it's a big variable and explains why they paid ~$500M above the 7x multiple for the extra capacity.

Next catalyst, possibly at closing or just after: a signed lease.

tweets.text:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

tweets.text:
High-income workers are fleeing Europe. 

Economic theory tells us that the more
mobile a factor of production becomes,
the lower its optimal tax rate. This is why taxes on capital, which is relatively mobile, tend to be lower than taxes on labor, which historically has been less mobile.

However, as the chart below shows, as elite human capital has become more footloose, high taxes have become increasingly counterproductive.

This is a huge existential problem for European welfare states, which have traditionally relied on heavily taxing their most productive workers.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. U.S. stocks had a powerful post-election rally on today, with the Dow Jones surging more than 3%, its strongest day since April 2025, as investors welcomed the removal of election uncertainty following Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress. The biggest catalyst was a sharp collapse in oil prices, driven by expectations that the new political landscape could increase pressure to resolve the Iran conflict, potentially easing energy costs, reducing inflationary pressures, and improving the outlook for consumers and businesses. Mega-cap technology stocks, including Amazon $AMZN, Microsoft $MSFT, Apple $AAPL, and Alphabet $GOOGL, rallied as falling Treasury yields and improving risk appetite supported equities. However, the semiconductor and AI infrastructure sectors moved sharply in the opposite direction, with Micron $MU, Sandisk $SNDK, Marvell $MRVL, and CoreWeave $CRWV facing significant selling pressure. Investors are increasingly concerned that a Democratic Congress could introduce stricter data center regulations, permitting restrictions, and higher costs for AI infrastructure development, potentially slowing the pace of capital investment. 

2. President Donald Trump said he is not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, while defending his administration's military campaign against Iran following Republican losses in the midterm elections. Trump acknowledged that it was “largely true” that Republicans lost because of the Iran war, citing the impact of surging oil and gasoline prices on voters. However, when asked whether the conflict was worth the political and economic consequences, Trump responded “yes,” arguing that the United States had little choice because Iran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. On the possibility of ending the conflict, Trump declared that “the Iran war will end whenever I want it to,” signaling that he believes the timing of any conclusion remains under his control. 

3. Uber $UBER delivered strong Q3 2026 earnings, with revenue increasing 10% YoY to $14.8B, beating the $14.69B estimate, while adjusted EPS surged 35% to $0.88, exceeding expectations of $0.86. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 31% to $2.96B, ahead of consensus, while free cash flow reached $2.54B, highlighting continued profitability and cash generation. Gross bookings climbed 20% to $59.82B, supported by 215M monthly active platform consumers, up 14% YoY, and 4.1B trips, up 16%. By segment, Delivery revenue surged 23% to $5.49B, Freight revenue increased 34% to $1.76B, while Mobility revenue declined 2% to $7.52B. Looking ahead, Uber guided Q4 adjusted EBITDA to $3.13B–$3.23B, with gross bookings of $63.25B–$65.25B and adjusted EPS of $0.95–$0.99. Management also highlighted accelerating progress in autonomous transportation, expecting approximately 700 fully driverless vehicles operating on Uber's platform by year-end and more than 2,000 in 2027, as the company increasingly focuses on commercializing robotaxi services at scale.

4. AMD $AMD has dramatically increased its unconditional purchase commitments to $48.8B, up 4x from $12.2B at the end of 2025 and $30.3B in June, according to its latest 10-Q filing, highlighting the enormous supply chain investments required to support its accelerating AI infrastructure business. Approximately $33.4B of these commitments are due by the end of 2027, primarily covering semiconductor wafers, advanced memory, substrates, and packaging capacity. AMD also disclosed $6.2B in cloud computing commitments, $13.3B in data center leases it expects to assign or sublease to partners, and up to $8.5B in guarantees covering partners' lease and debt obligations. Notably, lease guarantees nearly doubled to $7.7B from $4.1B in June, although AMD reported no partner defaults or guarantee payments to date. 

5. Alphabet $GOOGL plans to invest $15B in Malaysia during 2027 and 2028, significantly expanding its presence in Southeast Asia through new data center campuses, clean energy infrastructure, water security initiatives, and workforce training programs, according to Reuters. The investment highlights Google's accelerating commitment to AI and cloud computing infrastructure as demand for computing capacity continues to grow across the region. Beyond data center construction, the initiative will focus on securing reliable electricity, sustainable water resources, and skilled workers needed to support large-scale AI operations. 

6. Oracle $ORCL has reportedly canceled a $7B AI chip leasing agreement with Chinese technology giant Tencent following pressure from the Trump administration, according to the Financial Times. The proposed five-year agreement would have provided Tencent access to as many as 100,000 advanced AI chips housed in Oracle data centers across Southeast Asia, representing Tencent's largest overseas AI computing arrangement. The deal would have allowed Tencent to access advanced semiconductor technology that remains restricted within China, prompting U.S. officials to raise national security concerns with Oracle. Meanwhile, senior Chinese officials reportedly urged Tencent to prioritize domestic semiconductor suppliers, adding pressure from Beijing. Although overseas AI chip leasing remains permitted under existing regulations, the agreement was reportedly abandoned amid mounting geopolitical pressure from both governments. 

7. Coherent $COHR delivered a strong Q1 FY2027 earnings beat, with revenue surging 50% YoY to $2.37B, exceeding the $2.31B estimate, while adjusted EPS jumped 80% to $2.09, beating expectations of $1.97. Non-GAAP operating income reached $550M, ahead of the $527M estimate, while gross margins expanded 184 basis points to 40.6%, reflecting improving profitability. The standout was Data Center & Communications revenue, which surged 79% YoY to $1.95B, exceeding the $1.86B estimate, driven by accelerating demand for optical networking and AI infrastructure connectivity, while Industrial revenue declined 15% to $418.6M. Looking ahead, Coherent guided Q2 adjusted EPS to $2.28–$2.48, above the $2.21 consensus, with expected gross margins of 40%–42%. Management also expects FY2027 pro forma revenue growth to exceed 60% and anticipates achieving its first quarter with non-GAAP gross margins above 45% before the end of 2028, highlighting continued operating leverage as AI data center demand accelerates.

8. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $NVDA with 6.3M contracts, $AAPL with 4.7M contracts, $TSLA with 4.0M contracts, $INTC with 2.4M contracts, $AMZN with 2.2M contracts, $MU with 2.2M contracts, $AMD with 1.4M contracts, $PLTR with 1.2M contracts, $SPCX with 1.2M contracts, and $GOOGL with 1.1M contracts.

9. Intel $INTC CEO Lip-Bu Tan purchased 150,000 shares of Intel stock on November 2 at an average price of approximately $64.73 per share, representing a personal investment of roughly $9.7M, according to an SEC filing. The sizable insider purchase represents a notable vote of confidence from Intel's chief executive as the company continues executing its turnaround strategy, expanding its AI and data center business, and investing in its next-generation foundry manufacturing capabilities. The transaction highlights Tan's willingness to increase his personal exposure to Intel's long-term performance as investors assess the sustainability of its recovery.

10. Big Tech stock buybacks are collapsing as AI infrastructure spending takes priority, with combined share repurchases by Alphabet $GOOGL, Amazon $AMZN, Microsoft $MSFT, Meta $META, and Oracle $ORCL reportedly falling to just $4.4B in Q3 2026, their lowest quarterly level since Q3 2017. That represents a staggering 90% decline from the $45.9B peak recorded in Q4 2021, highlighting a major shift in how America's largest technology companies allocate capital. The slowdown comes as hyperscalers commit hundreds of billions of dollars toward AI data centers, GPUs, networking equipment, and power infrastructure, increasingly prioritizing capacity expansion over returning cash to shareholders. The trend signals a significant transformation in Big Tech's capital allocation strategy, with AI investments absorbing cash that might otherwise have supported stock repurchases, potentially reducing an important source of demand for their shares.

11. Goldman Sachs $GS and Apollo Global Management $APO have reportedly begun marketing portions of SpaceX's $SPCX massive $40B AI chip financing package to institutional investors, with individual allocations reaching as much as $500M, according to Bloomberg. The transaction, described as the largest GPU financing arrangement on record, involves an Apollo-backed entity purchasing approximately $47.3B in NVIDIA $NVDA GPUs and related equipment, primarily next-generation Rubin chips, funded through roughly $40B in debt and a $7B lease prepayment from SpaceX. The debt package includes an $8.3B senior-secured loan alongside multiple bond tranches, with the financing structured so that the Apollo-backed entity owns the equipment while SpaceX leases the GPUs for approximately five years. The arrangement is designed to keep the financing debt off SpaceX's balance sheet, although the company remains obligated to make lease payments even if equipment is damaged or operations are disrupted. 

12. South Korea's exports surged an extraordinary 94% YoY in October to $115B, marking the second-highest monthly total on record and the fastest annual growth rate since January 1974. The country has now recorded five consecutive months of export growth exceeding 60%, bringing total exports during the first 10 months of 2026 to a record $930B. The acceleration was overwhelmingly driven by semiconductors, with chip exports skyrocketing 259% YoY to a record $56B, while computer exports surged 497% amid explosive global demand for AI servers and computing infrastructure. The figures highlight South Korea's increasingly critical role in the global AI hardware supply chain, particularly through memory manufacturers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, as hyperscalers continue investing heavily in data centers, advanced memory, and next-generation computing systems.

WALL STREET IS THE GREATEST SHOW ON EARTH.
